name: Smooth PEI (laminated sheet on spring steel)
summary: A flat, unfilled polyetherimide (PEI/Ultem-class) film laminated to a flexible spring-steel carrier — or, on budget builds, bonded to glass or aluminium with 3M 468MP adhesive. Amber, glossy, and high-Tg (~217 degC), it gives the flattest and shiniest print bottoms of any PEI finish. Its bond strength is the highest of the family, which is a feature for PLA and a liability for PETG, TPU and PC, all of which can chemically weld to it and tear the film on release.
surface_makeup: Unfilled polyetherimide (PEI/Ultem-class amorphous thermoplastic) film, laminated to spring steel or adhered to glass/aluminium with 3M 468MP transfer tape; the gloss comes from the polished lamination, not a coating

filament_compatibility.notes: The reference use case: strong direct bond, glossiest and flattest bottom surface of any PEI finish.

preparation: On first use, wash the sheet with warm water and unscented dish soap (or a heavy 99% IPA wipe) to strip factory mould-release and handling oils, then dry completely with a clean paper towel. In routine use, wipe with 90%+ IPA on a lint-free cloth before every print, or at least every few prints — smooth PEI shows fingerprints as adhesion dropouts faster than textured surfaces because there is no micro-texture to compensate. When IPA stops restoring first-layer grip, escalate to a soapy-water wash; when soap stops working, a very light scuff with #0000 steel wool (uniform, whole-surface, never localised) restores tooth. Handle the sheet by its edges or tabs, and re-run first-layer/Live-Z calibration after swapping from a textured or satin sheet, since coating thickness differs.
cleaning: Routine cleaning is a cold 90-99% IPA wipe with a lint-free cloth or paper towel. Deep cleaning is warm water plus unscented dish soap, scrubbed with a soft sponge or cloth, rinsed and dried completely before the sheet goes back on the magnet — trapped water under a magnetic sheet causes corrosion of the steel carrier. Do not use acetone: Prusa and multiple plate vendors state it deteriorates PEI surfaces, and on laminated film it can also attack the adhesive layer. Skip abrasive scouring pads, wire brushes and metal scrapers, all of which leave scratches that become permanent adhesion dead-zones. Baked-on filament from a crashed Z-offset is best softened by heating the bed to that material's bed temperature and lifting the residue with a plastic scraper rather than cutting at it cold.
model_removal: Smooth PEI is a cold-release surface: let the bed drop to room temperature (below roughly 40 degC) so the differential contraction between the steel/PEI stack and the printed polymer breaks the bond, then lift the flexible sheet off the magnet and flex it in both directions until the part cracks free. Unlike textured plates, smooth PEI rarely self-releases on cooling — expect to flex actively, and expect large flat PLA or PETG footprints to need progressive flexing from one corner across the part. Use a plastic or nylon spatula only for stubborn small parts and only at a shallow angle to a corner; a metal blade will gouge the film and every gouge is a future adhesion failure. Never pry a part off a hot plate: the bond is at its strongest at temperature and that is when film tearing happens.
stuck_print_recovery: First, be patient — put the sheet aside and let it reach true room temperature, which resolves most cases. If the part still will not budge, put the whole flexible plate (print attached) in a freezer for 10-20 minutes; the further contraction differential pops most prints free. For PETG, PC and ASA parts that have chemically bonded, drip 90%+ IPA at the print/plate interface and let it wick underneath for a minute or two to break the bond, repeating at several edges (skip this on PVB, which IPA dissolves). Mechanically, unwaxed dental floss or a thin steel wire sawed under a corner and drawn across the footprint is far gentler on the film than a scraper. If nothing works, reheat the bed to the material's print bed temperature, then let it cool fully and undisturbed and retry — but do not shock a hot plate with ice or cold water, which can crack the film or delaminate it from the steel.

damage_avoidance.reason: Disputed and sheet-dependent. Prusa's own smooth-sheet page permits acetone once or twice a month when IPA is no longer sufficient, while Prusa prohibits it outright on its coated satin and textured sheets, and most plate vendors repeat a blanket 'no acetone' rule for the PEI family. Bulk PEI resin tolerates alcohols and aliphatics well, but this plate is a thin film over 3M 468MP-class transfer adhesive: solvent that runs to an edge wicks into that adhesive layer and starts delamination, which is the failure the blanket rule is really guarding against. Treat occasional whole-surface use as the outer limit and keep it off the edges.

damage_avoidance.item: Metal scrapers, razor blades and wire brushes
damage_avoidance.reason: The working surface is an unfilled PEI film only a few tenths of a millimetre thick. A blade gouges through it in one pass, and every gouge becomes a permanent adhesion dead-zone that prints will lift from for the rest of the sheet's life. There is no fill-and-polish repair path on a laminated film.

damage_avoidance.item: Coarse abrasives, scouring pads and localised scrubbing
damage_avoidance.reason: Not the same as sanctioned restoration. Prusa documents reviving smooth PEI with light, uniform 600-1000 grit sanding, and this catalogue records the equivalent #0000 steel-wool pass, both of which bring fresh PEI to the surface. What kills the sheet is coarse or localised abrasion: scouring pads and spot-scrubbing a stubborn patch cut a shallow crater that reads as a permanently different Z datum and a locally different gloss.

damage_avoidance.item: Prying parts off while the plate is hot
damage_avoidance.reason: Smooth PEI's bond is at maximum strength at bed temperature; that is exactly when the film tears rather than releases. Cold release plus flexing the sheet off the magnet is the intended workflow, and hot removal is the single most common way a smooth sheet is ruined in its first month.

damage_avoidance.item: Ice, cold water or a wet cloth on a hot plate
damage_avoidance.reason: Thermal shocking a hot laminated stack cracks the PEI film and can pop it loose from the steel at the adhesive line. Note this is not the same as the freezer trick, which is applied to a fully cooled sheet and is standard community practice on smooth PEI; Prusa nonetheless discourages freezing its coated sheets, so the guidance is construction-dependent rather than universal.

damage_avoidance.item: IPA on or near PVB prints
damage_avoidance.reason: IPA is the routine cleaner here and is harmless to the film, but PVB is IPA-soluble, so wicking alcohol under a PVB footprint softens the print into a gum that smears into the surface and then has to be washed out with soap and water before adhesion returns. Use water and patience on PVB instead.

damage_avoidance.item: Bar soap, scented or moisturising soaps, and bare-hand handling
damage_avoidance.reason: Prusa's instruction is explicit: do not use anything made for skin, because it contains oils that ruin adhesion. Skin oils themselves are worse on smooth PEI than on any textured surface, because there is no micro-texture to key into around a fingerprint, so the contaminated patch simply fails. Deep cleaning wants plain unscented dish soap and handling by the tabs.

Combines everything the sheet dislikes: alkaline detergent with abrasive builders against a soft film, a long hot-and-humid dry cycle against the exposed spring-steel carrier, and water forced into the film-to-steel bond line. Prusa forum consensus is hand-washing with immediate drying; one member's single-cycle test showed no immediate harm, but nobody published long-term results.

damage_avoidance.item: Repeated hard flexing, especially of thin budget sheets
damage_avoidance.reason: Flexing is the intended release mechanism, but bowing the whole sheet aggressively rather than working progressively from a corner permanently warps thin steel. A sheet that no longer lies flat cannot be recovered by cleaning and shows up as first-layer variation across large footprints long before the PEI itself wears out.

The polymer is not the limit here; the lamination is. PEI resin has continuous service well above any FDM bed temperature, but the 3M-class transfer adhesive holding the film to the steel softens first, showing up as bubbling, edge lift or a sheet that will not sit flat. No vendor publishes a rated maximum for a laminated sheet, so the ceiling recorded in this entry is a conservative estimate rather than a datasheet figure.

lifespan_notes: Expect roughly 12-18 months of regular daily use before adhesion becomes unreliable, per Bambu-ecosystem community reporting; light users get several years. Wear shows up as scratches, locally shiny or hazed patches, and areas of the bed that work while others fail. The usual accelerators are metal scrapers, acetone or other aggressive solvents, baked-on filament from a bad Z-offset, and repeated hard flexing of thin budget steel, which eventually leaves the sheet visibly non-flat. There is no practical home recoating path — the sheet is a consumable and gets replaced; a few third-party PEI relamination services exist but are not mainstream (unverified).

price.notes: Prusa smooth PEI sheet about USD 35 in the 250x220 mm class; Bambu Smooth PEI Plate roughly USD 25-30 (unverified, store page inaccessible at time of research); FYSETC/BIQU double-sided smooth+textured steel sheets USD 20-30 for 235-310 mm sizes.

additional_notes: Almost always sold as one face of a double-sided sheet (smooth on one side, textured or satin on the other) and mounted on a magnetic base, so a single purchase covers two finishes and swaps tool-free across Bambu, Prusa MK3S+/MK4/CORE One and Creality machines. Chosen when a part needs a flat, glossy reference face. Do not confuse smooth PEI with PEO/PEY holographic films (see pei-patterned) — those are different, lower-temperature polymers marketed under similar 'PEI' language. Long-term flatness is the quiet failure mode on cheap thin sheets: repeated heat cycling curls the edges before the PEI itself gives out.

provenance.conflicts: Surface thermal ceiling is unverified: PEI resin datasheets imply continuous service well above 150 degC, but no vendor publishes a rated max bed temperature for a laminated sheet, and the 3M-class adhesive or steel lamination is the real limit rather than the polymer — the 150 degC max recorded here is a conservative estimate, not a published figure. Bambu's Smooth PEI Plate price (USD 25-30) could not be confirmed against the manufacturer store. Sources also disagree on removal aids: general community practice endorses the freezer trick on smooth PEI, while Prusa discourages freezer use for its coated sheets, so the guidance differs by sheet construction rather than being universal. Vendor ratings for TPU and PC range from flat 'avoid' to 'fine with a glue stick'; recorded here as usable-with-prep with a mandatory separator, which is the conservative reading.
